  A numeracy program field-tests every new item, and wants to know whether
  item difficulty can be predicted from the text instead. Describe 192
  items by their text features, compare an explanatory model with machine

  and cannot replace. About 75 minutes.

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(mirtverse)
tutorial_options(exercise.checker = mirtverse::lab_checker,
                 exercise.timelimit = 120, exercise.lines = 6)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5)
```

```{r setup-feat, include = FALSE}
feats <- item_features(itemtext)
items <- merge(itemtext, feats)
text <- c("words", "sentences", "grade", "numbers", "max_digits", "decimals",
          "option_words", "key_longest", "distractor_distance")
```

```{r setup-clean, include = FALSE}
feats <- item_features(itemtext)
items <- merge(itemtext, feats)
text <- c("words", "sentences", "grade", "numbers", "max_digits", "decimals",
          "option_words", "key_longest", "distractor_distance")
clean <- items[items$a > 0, ]
```

## The brief

### Two hundred new items a year

You are the psychometrician for the fictional **Prairie Grade 7 Numeracy
Assessment**. Every year its item writers produce about 200 new
multiple-choice items, and every item is field-tested on 1,500 students
before it can be used. Field testing is the program's slowest step, and it
exposes items a year before they count.

The items are written from **item models**: Templates such as *"What is
p% of x?"* or *"A car travels d km in t hours. What is its average
speed?"*, filled with different numbers, names and contexts. A vendor says
its software can predict an item's difficulty from its text. The director
asks you:

> *Can we predict how hard an item is before anyone answers it? Could that
> shrink, or even replace, the field test?*

Last year's 192 field-tested items are in `itemtext`, with their text and
their 2PL estimates.

### Meet the data

Each row is an item: Its `id` (family and item number), its `family` (the
item model), the `stem`, the options `A` to `D` and the `key`, and the
field-test results: Difficulty `b`, discrimination `a`, their standard
errors, and `p_field`, the share of students who answered correctly.

```{r look, exercise = TRUE}
head(itemtext[, c("id", "family", "stem", "key", "b")], 4)
itemtext$stem[c(1, 2, 70)]
round(sort(tapply(itemtext$b, itemtext$family, mean)), 2)
```

```{r look-check}
"192 items from 12 item models. Families differ a lot in difficulty: Converting units is the easiest and Solving equations the hardest."
```

## Features from the text

### What the text says about an item

`item_features()` reads each stem and its options and returns features:
Length (`words`, `sentences`), readability (`grade`), the `numbers` and the
digits of the largest one (`max_digits`), whether the stem or the key uses
`decimals` or fractions, the length of the options, whether the key is the
longest option, how far the distractors are from the key, and each item's
most similar other item. Join them to the items:

```{r feat, exercise = TRUE}
feats <- item_features(itemtext)
items <- merge(itemtext, feats)
items[c(1, 2, 70), c("id", "words", "sentences", "max_digits", "decimals", "similarity", "nearest")]
```

```{r feat-check}
lab_need(exists("items") && is.data.frame(items) && nrow(items) == 192 && "similarity" %in% names(items),
         "Keep the names `feats` and `items`, and merge the features into the items.")
"Each item now has its text features next to its field-test results."
```

### Near-duplicates

Items written from the same template look alike, but two items that differ
only in a name are the same item, and should never appear on the same form.
List the items whose most similar other item has a `similarity` above 0.8.

```{r dup, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-feat"}
twins <- feats[feats$similarity > , c("id", "nearest", "similarity")]
twins
```

```{r dup-hint}
twins <- feats[feats$similarity > 0.8, c("id", "nearest", "similarity")]
```

```{r dup-solution}
twins <- feats[feats$similarity > 0.8, c("id", "nearest", "similarity")]
twins
```

```{r dup-check}
lab_need(exists("twins") && is.data.frame(twins) && "nearest" %in% names(twins),
         "Keep the name `twins` and the columns id, nearest and similarity.")
lab_need(nrow(twins) == 4, "Use a similarity above 0.8: Four items, two pairs.")
"Two pairs stand out: N01-02 and N01-14, and N06-05 and N06-12. Read their stems: Each pair differs only in a name. The next most similar items are well below, at about 0.6."
```

```{r q-dup}
question_radio("What should the program do about the two pairs?",
  answer("Treat each pair as one item: Mark them as enemies so they never appear on the same form, and keep only one of each in the bank.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right. A changed name does not make a new item. Near-duplicates also flatter a difficulty model: If one twin is in training and the other is predicted, the model looks better than it is."),
  answer("Nothing; they have different ids, so they are different items.",
         message = "Their ids differ, but a student who has seen one has seen the other. Different ids are a bookkeeping fact, not evidence of different content."),
  answer("Delete both items.",
         message = "There is nothing wrong with either item on its own. Keep one and record the pair."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## A first model

### Predicting difficulty from the text

`predict_difficulty()` predicts `b` from features with three models: An
**LLTM**, the explanatory linear model of psychometrics; a **lasso**, the
same model with its weights shrunk; and a **random forest**. Each is judged
by 5-fold cross-validation: Every item is predicted by a model that did not
see it. The setup has stored the names of nine text features in `text`.
Run the models, giving the standard errors of `b` as `se`.

```{r first, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-feat", exercise.timelimit = 180}
text
first <- predict_difficulty(items, text, se = )
first
autoplot(first)
```

```{r first-hint}
first <- predict_difficulty(items, text, se = "___")
```

```{r first-solution}
text
first <- predict_difficulty(items, text, se = "b_se")
first
autoplot(first)
```

```{r first-check}
lab_need(exists("first") && inherits(first, "mv_difficulty"),
         "Keep the name `first` and use predict_difficulty().")
lab_need(identical(first$se, "b_se"), "Give the standard errors of b: se = \"b_se\".")
acc <- first$accuracy
sprintf("Not impressive: The LLTM explains %.0f%% of the variance in b, the forest %.0f%%. And three items have estimated difficulties far below anything the models predict, by 3 logits or more. They are labelled in the plot.",
        100 * acc$r2[acc$method == "lltm"], 100 * acc$r2[acc$method == "forest"])
```

### The three worst items

Look at the three worst-predicted items: N05-07, N08-11 and N11-03.

```{r worst, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-feat"}
worst <- items[items$id %in% c("N05-07", "N08-11", "N11-03"), ]
worst[, c("id", "stem", "A", "B", "C", "D", "key", "a", "b", "p_field")]
```

```{r worst-check}
"Look at a, b and p_field, and work out each item's correct answer."
```

```{r q-worst}
question_radio("What is wrong with these three items?",
  answer("They are miskeyed, and because few students choose the listed key, the items are estimated to be very hard.",
         message = "Read b again: It is very low, as if the items were very easy, although only 11% to 17% are scored correct. The negative discrimination flips the curve."),
  answer("They are miskeyed: The listed key is wrong, so the strongest students, who choose the correct answer, are marked wrong. The discrimination is negative, which turns the b estimate into nonsense.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right. Check the key, rescore the field test, and recalibrate. A difficulty model is also a quality check: Items it cannot explain at all are worth a second look."),
  answer("They are simply very hard items that the text features cannot explain.",
         message = "Only 11% to 17% answered 'correctly', yet b says the items are very easy, and a is negative. That is not difficulty; it is a scoring error."),
  answer("The model is wrong for these items, so a random forest should be used.",
         message = "No model should predict these b values: They are not difficulties. The data need fixing first."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## The vendor's model

### Too good to be true?

Set the three miskeyed items aside until they are rescored: Keep the items
with a positive discrimination. The vendor's spreadsheet also uses
`p_field`. Add it to the text features and see how well the models do now.

```{r vendor, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-feat", exercise.timelimit = 180}
clean <- items[items$a > , ]
vendor <- predict_difficulty(clean, c(text, "p_field"), se = "b_se")
vendor
```

```{r vendor-hint}
clean <- items[items$a > 0, ]
```

```{r vendor-solution}
clean <- items[items$a > 0, ]
vendor <- predict_difficulty(clean, c(text, "p_field"), se = "b_se")
vendor
```

```{r vendor-check}
lab_need(exists("clean") && is.data.frame(clean) && nrow(clean) == 189,
         "`clean` should hold the 189 items with a positive discrimination: items$a > 0.")
lab_need(exists("vendor") && inherits(vendor, "mv_difficulty"),
         "Keep the name `vendor` and use predict_difficulty().")
acc <- vendor$accuracy
sprintf("Spectacular: R2 of %.2f, an error of %.2f logits. And a warning about p_field.",
        acc$r2[acc$method == "lltm"], acc$rmse[acc$method == "lltm"])
```

```{r q-leak}
question_radio("Why can the program not use the vendor's model?",
  answer("p_field is the proportion correct in the field test, computed from the same responses as b. A new item has no field-test data, so the model needs the very thing it is supposed to replace.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right: Data leakage. A feature that would not be available when the prediction is needed must not be used to build or judge the model, however well it predicts."),
  answer("The model overfits: R2 values above 0.9 are impossible.",
         message = "High R2 values are possible. The problem is where p_field comes from."),
  answer("The lasso and forest disagree with the LLTM.",
         message = "They agree closely. The problem is the feature, not the models."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## Text alone

### An honest model

Now predict difficulty from the text features alone, on the clean items.

```{r textonly, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-clean", exercise.timelimit = 180}
honest <- predict_difficulty(clean, text, se = "b_se")
honest
```

```{r textonly-check}
lab_need(exists("honest") && inherits(honest, "mv_difficulty") && !"p_field" %in% honest$features,
         "Keep the name `honest`, with the text features only.")
acc <- honest$accuracy
sprintf("The linear models explain about %.0f%% of the variance; the random forest about %.0f%%, with an error of %.2f logits.",
        100 * mean(acc$r2[acc$method != "forest"]), 100 * acc$r2[acc$method == "forest"],
        acc$rmse[acc$method == "forest"])
```

```{r q-forest}
question_radio("Why does the forest do so much better than the linear models with the same features?",
  answer("Items from the same item model share their wording and the size of their numbers, so a combination of features identifies the family. The forest learns which family an item belongs to, and the family carries most of the difficulty.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right. The forest is not reading difficulty off the text; it is recognizing the template. That works only for families it has already seen, which is worth testing."),
  answer("Random forests are always more accurate than linear models.",
         message = "Not always: In the book's chapter the linear models win. Here the forest has something to recognize."),
  answer("The forest overfits, so its cross-validated R2 is wrong.",
         message = "The R2 is computed on items the forest did not see, so overfitting would lower it, not raise it."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## Item models

### Adding the family

If the family carries most of the difficulty, give it to the models
directly.

```{r family, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-clean", exercise.timelimit = 180}
fam <- predict_difficulty(clean, c("family", text), se = "b_se")
fam
```

```{r family-check}
lab_need(exists("fam") && inherits(fam, "mv_difficulty") && "family" %in% fam$features,
         "Keep the name `fam`, with the family and the text features.")
acc <- fam$accuracy
sprintf("Now all three models explain about %.0f%% of the variance, with an error of about %.2f logits. The estimation error in b alone is 0.07.",
        100 * mean(acc$r2), mean(acc$rmse))
```

### A new family

Random folds always keep some items of every family in training. A new
item model is a different question. Hold out whole families: Set `group`
to the family column.

```{r newfam, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-clean", exercise.timelimit = 180}
newfam <- predict_difficulty(clean, c("family", text), se = "b_se", group = )
newfam
```

```{r newfam-hint}
newfam <- predict_difficulty(clean, c("family", text), se = "b_se", group = "___")
```

```{r newfam-solution}
newfam <- predict_difficulty(clean, c("family", text), se = "b_se", group = "family")
newfam
```

```{r newfam-check}
lab_need(exists("newfam") && inherits(newfam, "mv_difficulty"),
         "Keep the name `newfam` and use predict_difficulty().")
lab_need(identical(newfam$group, "family"), "Hold out whole families: group = \"family\".")
acc <- newfam$accuracy
sprintf("For a family none of the models has seen, R2 is %.2f at best: Worse than predicting the average difficulty for every item.",
        max(acc$r2))
```

```{r q-newfam}
question_radio("What can the program claim about predicted difficulties?",
  answer("For a new item from an item model that has been calibrated, the prediction is close to what a field test would give. For a new item model, the text says almost nothing about difficulty, and the items need a full field test.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right: The unit you hold out decides what you can claim. This is the logic of automatic item generation: Calibrate the item model, then predict its new items."),
  answer("Predictions are accurate for any new item: R2 was about 0.9.",
         message = "Only when the item's family was in training. With whole families held out, the models do worse than a constant."),
  answer("Predictions are useless, because they fail for new families.",
         message = "Most new items come from existing item models, and for them the predictions are good."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## What makes items harder?

### Reading the LLTM

Within a family, what does the wording add? Fit the LLTM alone with the
family and three features, and read its weights.

```{r effects, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "setup-clean"}
eff <- predict_difficulty(clean, c("family", "sentences", "max_digits", "decimals"),
                          se = "b_se", methods = "lltm")
w <- tidy(eff)
w[!grepl("family", w$term), ]
```

```{r effects-check}
w <- tidy(eff)
sprintf("An extra sentence adds about %.2f logits and decimals or fractions about %.2f; the size of the largest number in the stem adds little (%.2f per digit).",
        w$estimate[w$term == "sentences"], w$estimate[w$term == "decimals"],
        w$estimate[w$term == "max_digits"])
```

```{r q-effects}
question_radio("In most families, the extra sentence is a context sentence such as \"Maya is buying supplies for a school trip.\", which adds nothing to the mathematics. What does its weight of about 0.14 logits mean for the test?",
  answer("Reading load makes items slightly harder, apart from the mathematics. That is construct-irrelevant difficulty, which may matter most for weaker readers and English language learners: Worth checking with a DIF analysis.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Right. An explanatory model turns a prediction into a question about the construct, which is exactly what item writers and fairness reviewers need."),
  answer("Nothing; 0.14 logits is too small to matter.",
         message = "Small for one item, but it applies to every item with a context sentence, and it may not be the same for every group of students."),
  answer("Context sentences should be added to every item to make the test harder.",
         message = "They make items harder by adding reading, not mathematics. That changes what the test measures."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

## The recommendation

```{r q-deploy}
question_radio("What do you recommend to the director?",
  answer("Use predicted difficulties for new items from calibrated item models to build targeted field-test forms and to cut field-test samples, but keep a smaller field test for every item, and give new item models a full one. Check keys and near-duplicates before calibration, and re-check the predictions each year.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "A defensible plan: It saves field-test students, the claims match the evidence, and every operational difficulty is still estimated from responses."),
  answer("Replace the field test: Predictions are within about 0.2 logits.",
         message = "Only for known item models, and a field test also catches miskeys, which no text model can. Shrink it; do not drop it."),
  answer("Buy the vendor's software.",
         message = "The vendor's accuracy came from p_field, a feature that only exists after the field test."),
  answer("Ignore difficulty prediction; field-test everything as before.",
         message = "Safe, but it gives up real savings for items from calibrated item models."),
  allow_retry = TRUE, random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

### Write to the director

Write a short memo (four to six sentences): How well difficulty can be
predicted from the text, for which items, what you found in the data, and
what you recommend.

```{r q-memo}
question_text(
  "Your memo:",
  answer_fn(function(value) {
    if (nchar(trimws(value)) < 120)
      return(incorrect("Write a bit more: Cover the accuracy, which items it applies to, the problems you found and your recommendation."))
    correct("Submitted. Now see what was planted in the data.")
  }),
  correct = "Submitted.", allow_retry = TRUE, rows = 8,
  placeholder = "To the director: ..."
)
```

## The reveal

### What was planted in the items

`itemtext` was simulated from 12 item models. Each item's true difficulty
is its family's difficulty plus effects of its surface features and some
item-specific noise. `lab_truth("itemtext")` lists what was built in.

```{r truth, exercise = TRUE}
truth <- lab_truth("itemtext")
truth$effects
truth$miskeyed
truth$near_duplicates
truth$leaky
```

| What was planted | What you found |
|---|---|
| Family difficulties from -1.25 to 1.0 logits | The family carries most of the difficulty; new families cannot be predicted |
| Decimals or fractions +0.35, each extra digit +0.12, a context sentence +0.15 | The LLTM recovers the context effect; the text features are only proxies for the rest |
| Item-specific noise, SD 0.20 | With the family, the error of about 0.22 logits is close to this floor |
| Three miskeyed items | Negative discrimination and absurd b; the worst-predicted items |
| Two near-duplicate pairs (a changed name) | Similarity of 0.87 and 0.92, far above the next pair |
| `p_field` from the same field test as `b` | R2 of 0.97 that would vanish for new items |

The best possible model, with the true features, would still miss each
item by about 0.2 logits: Item-specific difficulty that no feature of the
text explains. Real items have more of it than these simulated ones.

tableOutput("decision_log")
```

    "q-worst" = "The three worst items",
    "q-leak" = "The vendor's model",
    "q-forest" = "Why the forest wins on text alone",
    "q-newfam" = "What predictions can claim",
    "q-effects" = "The context sentence",
    "q-deploy" = "Recommendation",

  ))
})
```

You have predicted item difficulty from text the way a testing program
should: Without leaked features, on the right held-out unit, with the data
checked first, and with an explanatory model that says what makes items
hard.
